interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the hoop's flux halve, with the coil's field still at 5 mT, when you tilt the hoop 60° from square-on.
interactive.title: The grip and the hoop
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Twelve small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and seven ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. Three buttons above it, Wire, Loop and Coil, and a current slider from 20 A one way, through zero, to 20 A the other, opening at 10 A. Wire: a wire seen end-on in the middle. A cross on it means the current flows into the page, away from you. A dot means it flows out, towards you. Eight compass needles stand in a ring round it, and field rings are drawn centred on the wire, closer together near it. For a current into the page the rings carry arrows running clockwise, and for one out of it anticlockwise. The needles turn to lie along them. At zero the rings vanish and the needles are drawn grey. One needle can be dragged out from the wire, from 5 mm to 50 mm, with a readout, Flux density at the needle, in mT. A small right hand by the wire shows the grip, its thumb along the current and its fingers curling with the rings.

Loop: the wire bent into one loop, cut through and seen side-on, a dot at the top and a cross at the bottom, each with its own rings. Inside the loop the rings from both sides point the same way and join. Coil: an air-cored coil, with a turns slider from 2 to 10 that stacks loops side by side. On Loop the turns slider stays in place, greyed out. Their rings join into lines running through the middle, out of one end and round the outside back into the other, as a bar magnet's do. The end the lines leave is labelled N and the end they return to S. The lines are drawn closer together in proportion to turns × current. Reversing the current turns every line round and swaps N and S.

The hoop. On Coil, a switch, Hoop, shows a hoop seen edge-on and hides the current and turns sliders. The coil is then held at one setting, where the flux density inside is 5 mT, say, and each line drawn stands for 1 µWb, say. The hoop can be dragged along the coil's axis from its middle to well past one end, and tilted from 0°, square-on to the lines, to 90°, edge-on, in steps of 15°. It has two sizes, 0.002 m² and 0.004 m². The lines it catches light up. Two readouts, which wrap onto two rows on a phone: Flux through the hoop, in µWb, and Flux density where it sits, in mT.

The rules it computes. Flux density B is flux ÷ area, with the area square-on to the lines. Inside the coil, 10 µWb through 0.002 m² gives 0.005 T, 5 mT, all along the middle. The flux through the hoop is Φ = B × A × cos θ, where θ is the tilt from square-on. Past the coil's end the lines spread out and the density falls, drawn as a sketch. Round the straight wire, B = μ₀ I ÷ 2πr, with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A. With B in mT and r in mm, μ₀ ÷ 2π comes to 0.2, so B in mT = 0.2 × current in A ÷ distance from the wire in mm.

Screen 1, show. The picture on Wire, 10 A into the page. The words: "A current makes a magnetic field. Here you see a wire end-on. The cross is the tail of the current's arrow, going away from you. A dot would be its point, coming towards you. Compass needles round the wire line up in circles centred on it.[^1] Grip the wire in your right hand with your thumb along the current. Your fingers curl the way the field goes. Drag the current down through zero. The rings fade to nothing, then come back turning the other way." Read: "With the current into the page, the needles line up in clockwise circles centred on the wire. At zero current the wire makes no field. Reverse the current, and the rings turn the other way." Still: Wire, 10 A into the page.

Screen 2, try it. "The current flows into the page, away from you. Which way does the needle just above the wire point?" Four choices, in this order, which wrap onto two rows on a phone: "Towards the wire"; "To the right"; "To the left"; "Away from the wire". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The field runs round the wire in rings. It never points at the wire." Hint for the third: "Point your right thumb into the page. Your fingers curl clockwise. Above the wire, they point right." Hint for the fourth: "Rings, not spokes. The needle lies along its ring." Why: "Point your right thumb along the current, into the page. Your fingers curl clockwise as you look. At the top of a clockwise ring, the field points right. The needle lies along it." A right Check lights the needle above the wire. Read: "The current flows into the page. Which way does the needle just above the wire point?"

Screen 3, show. The picture on Loop, then Coil. The words: "Switch to a loop, cut through and seen side-on. Its current comes out at the top and goes in at the bottom. Inside the loop, the rings from both sides point the same way, so they add. Add turns to make a coil. The rings join into lines through the middle and round the outside, like a bar magnet's field.[^2] Curl your right fingers along the current in the turns. Your thumb points to the north end, where the lines leave. More turns or more current crowd the lines closer." Read: "Inside a loop, the rings from its two sides add. A coil's rings join into a bar magnet's field. The lines leave from its north end. More turns or more current crowd them closer." Still: Coil, 6 turns, 10 A.

Screen 4, try it. "You look at one end of a coil. The current runs round it anticlockwise as you look. Is that end north or south?" Three choices, in this order: "South"; "North"; "Neither: only a bar magnet has poles". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "Curl your right fingers anticlockwise as you look. Your thumb points at you, out of this end." Hint for the third: "A coil's lines leave one end and go back in at the other, as a bar magnet's do." Why: "Curl your right fingers the way the current runs, anticlockwise as you look. Your thumb points out of the coil towards you. The lines leave that end, so it is north." A right Check turns the coil to show that end as N. Read: "You look at one end of a coil. The current runs round it anticlockwise. Is that end north or south?"

Screen 5, show. The picture on Coil with the Hoop on, square-on inside the coil, 0.002 m². The words: "Now hold a hoop inside the coil, square-on to the lines. The flux, Φ, is how much field threads it.[^3] It is measured in webers, Wb. Say each line drawn stands for 1 µWb, a millionth of a weber. This 0.002 m² hoop catches 10 lines, so 10 µWb. The flux density, B, is how crowded the lines are. It is the flux through each square metre, square-on. It is measured in teslas, T. Here B = 10 µWb ÷ 0.002 m² = 0.005 T, which is 5 mT." Read: "A 0.002 m² hoop, square-on inside the coil, catches 10 lines. That is 10 µWb. The flux density is 10 µWb ÷ 0.002 m² = 5 mT." Still: Hoop, 0.002 m², square-on, inside.

Screen 6, try it, typed. "Swap in a wider hoop, 0.004 m², square-on in the same 5 mT. What flux threads it?" A typed field in µWb, decimals allowed: answer 20, want "20 µWb". Slips: 10, "The field is the same, but a wider hoop catches more of it. Flux is density times area."; 20000, "5 mT is 0.005 T, not 5 T."; 0.02, "That is in milliwebers. The box is in microwebers." Hint for any other answer: "Multiply the density in teslas by the area in square metres." Why: "Flux is density times area. 0.005 T × 0.004 m² = 0.000 02 Wb, which is 20 µWb. Twice the area catches twice the flux at the same density." A right Check widens the hoop and lights 20 lines. Read: "A 0.004 m² hoop sits square-on in the same 5 mT. What flux threads it?"

Screen 7, show. The hoop back to 0.002 m², with the tilt to drag. The words: "Tilt the hoop. Its face now shows the lines a smaller area. Fewer lines thread it. At 60°, that area is cos 60° = 0.5 of the hoop. So the flux halves to 5 µWb. Edge-on, at 90°, it catches none. The field has not changed. Its density there is still 5 mT. So flux = B × area × cos of the tilt. Now drag the hoop out past the coil's end. The lines spread out there. So the density falls, and the flux falls with it." Read: "Tilted 60°, the hoop catches 5 µWb, half as much. The density stays 5 mT. Past the coil's end, the lines spread, so the density and the flux both fall." Still: Hoop, 0.002 m², tilted 60°, inside.

Screen 8, try it. "Tilting the hoop drops its flux from 10 µWb to 5 µWb. What has the coil's field done?" Three choices, in this order: "It has halved, to 2.5 mT"; "Nothing: the hoop catches less of the same field"; "It has turned to follow the hoop". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The coil's current and turns are the same, so its field is too. Only the hoop moved." Hint for the third: "The coil sets its field's lines. The hoop only catches them." Why: "Flux belongs to the hoop. It is how much field threads the hoop. The field belongs to the coil. Tilted, the hoop shows the lines a smaller face. So it catches less of the same 5 mT." Read: "Tilting the hoop drops its flux from 10 µWb to 5 µWb. What has the coil's field done?"

Screen 9, show. The picture back on Wire at 20 A, with the needle to drag. The words: "Back to the straight wire. Its flux density grows in step with the current. It falls in step with the distance. A ring twice as far out is twice as long. So the same field is spread twice as thin. In air, B = μ₀ I ÷ 2πr.[^4] Here μ₀ is the magnetic constant, 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A. With B in mT and r in mm, μ₀ ÷ 2π comes to 0.2. At 20 A and 10 mm, B = 0.2 × 20 ÷ 10 = 0.4 mT. Drag the needle out to 20 mm, and the density halves to 0.2 mT." Read: "With 20 A flowing, the flux density 10 mm from the wire is 0.4 mT. At 20 mm it is half that, 0.2 mT." Still: Wire, 20 A, needle at 20 mm.

Screen 10, try it, typed. "The same 20 A wire. What is the flux density 40 mm from it?" A typed field in mT, decimals allowed: answer 0.10, want "0.10 mT". Slips: 0.025, "That answer falls with the square of the distance, as light does. Round a long wire, the field falls in step with distance. Four times as far is a quarter as strong."; 0.4, "That is the density at 10 mm. Further out, the rings thin."; 1.6, "Further out the density falls, not rises." Hint for any other answer: "Use 0.2 × current in A ÷ distance in mm." Why: "0.2 × 20 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mT. 40 mm is four times as far as 10 mm. So the density is a quarter of 0.4 mT." A right Check drags the needle to 40 mm. Read: "A wire carries 20 A. What is the flux density 40 mm from it?"

Screen 11, try it, the first of two mixed puzzles, typed. "A hoop of 0.003 m² sits in an 8 mT field, tilted 60° from square-on. What flux threads it?" A typed field in µWb, decimals allowed: answer 12, want "12 µWb". Slips: 24, "That is the flux square-on. Tilted, the hoop shows the lines a smaller face."; 20.8, "That used sin 60°. Square-on is 0°, so the face shrinks by cos 60° = 0.5."; 12000, "8 mT is 0.008 T, not 8 T." Hint for any other answer: "Density × area × cos of the tilt." Why: "Square-on, 0.008 T × 0.003 m² = 0.000 024 Wb, which is 24 µWb. Tilted 60°, the hoop catches cos 60° = 0.5 of that, so 12 µWb." Read: "A 0.003 m² hoop sits in an 8 mT field, tilted 60° from square-on. What flux threads it?"

Screen 12, try it, the second mixed puzzle. "You reverse the current in a coil. What happens to its field?" Three choices, in this order: "Nothing: the winding fixes which end is north"; "Its north and south ends swap"; "It stays the same way round, only weaker". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The grip follows the current. Reverse it, and your thumb points the other way." Hint for the third: "The same current, reversed, makes the same strength of field, turned round." Why: "The field turns round with the current. The rings round the wire did the same through zero. Curl your fingers the new way, and your thumb points out of the other end. So north and south swap." A right Check reverses the coil's current. Read: "You reverse the current in a coil. What happens to its field?"

The finish. The words: "A current wraps rings of field round its wire, and your right-hand grip gives their way. A coil gathers them into a bar magnet's field, with north where the lines leave. Flux is how much of that field threads a hoop: density × area × cos of the tilt. Every contactor, relay and solenoid coil works by this field. Slide an iron core into the coil, and the same current makes far more flux. Why it does comes next."

Every figure on these screens is an example value or worked from the rules above.
interactive.ignores: The picture is flat. A real field fills the space round the wire and the coil. A round hoop catches lines over its whole face. So here a hoop of twice the area is drawn twice as long. The lines are a drawing. A real field is smooth, and 1 µWb a line is a scale chosen for the picture. The field inside the coil is drawn even. Past its end, its fall is a sketch. The needles follow the wire's field alone. Real compass needles also feel the Earth's field. Near a small current, they point somewhere between the two. The 0.2 rule is for a long straight wire in air, away from its ends and from iron.

explain.text:
A current makes a magnetic field. Round a straight wire, the field runs in rings centred on the wire.[^1] Wind the wire into a coil, and the rings join into a field like a bar magnet's.[^2] [[Flux]] is how much of that field threads a loop, such as a hoop you hold in it.

Grip a wire in your right hand with your thumb along the current. Your fingers curl the way the field goes. With the current going into the page, the rings run clockwise. So a needle just above the wire points right. It lies along its ring, not at the wire. Turn the current down, and the rings fade to nothing at zero. Past zero they come back, turning the other way. Now bend the wire into a loop. Inside it, the rings from the two sides point the same way, so they add. Stack loops into a coil, and every turn adds again. The lines run through the middle, out of one end and round the outside back into the other. The end they leave is north. Curl your right fingers along the current in the turns, and your thumb points to north. More turns or more current crowd the lines closer.

Now hold a hoop inside the coil, square-on to the lines. The flux, Φ, is the field that threads it. Only the part square-on to its face counts.[^3] The [[flux density]], B, is how crowded the lines are. It is the flux per square metre. Flux is measured in webers, Wb. Flux density is measured in teslas, T, where one tesla is one weber per square metre. Say a 0.002 m² hoop catches 10 µWb. Then B = Φ ÷ A = 10 µWb ÷ 0.002 m² = 5 mT. A hoop twice the area catches twice the flux, 20 µWb, from the same 5 mT. Tilt the hoop 60°, and its face shows the lines a smaller area. That area is cos 60° = 0.5 of the hoop, so it catches 5 µWb. The field has not changed. So Φ = B × A × cos θ, where θ is the tilt from square-on. Round a long straight wire, the density falls with distance. A ring twice as far out is twice as long, so the field is spread twice as thin. In air, B = μ₀ I ÷ 2πr, where μ₀ is the magnetic constant, 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A.[^4] With B in mT and r in mm, that comes to 0.2 × the current in amps ÷ the distance in mm. So 20 A gives 0.4 mT at 10 mm and 0.2 mT at 20 mm. The picture is a simplified model. It is flat, and it draws the field inside the coil as even. A real coil's field fills space and thins towards its ends.

Many current transformers are a ring of iron round a conductor. They gather the rings of field round that conductor. **A current wraps its wire in rings of field.[^1] They turn round when the current does. A coil gathers them into a bar magnet's field.[^2] Flux is how much of that field threads a loop, square-on to it.[^3] Flux density is that flux per square metre.**

analogy.text: Think of rain and a bucket. How hard the rain falls is the flux density. What the bucket catches is the flux. A wider bucket catches more of the same rain, and a tilted one catches less, though the rain has not changed.
analogy.breaks: Rain is water that moves and is used up when it is caught. A field does not flow and is not used up. Its lines carry on through the hoop and close on themselves round the coil.

practice.text:
- To find the field round a wire, point your right thumb along the current. Your fingers curl the way the field goes.
- To find a coil's north end, curl your right fingers along the current in its turns. Your thumb points north. Seen end-on, anticlockwise current means you are looking at north. Clockwise means south.
- To find flux, multiply the flux density by the area and by cos of the tilt: Φ = B × A × cos θ. The tilt is measured from square-on.
- To find flux density from a flux, divide by the area square-on to the lines: B = Φ ÷ A.
- Work in teslas, square metres and webers, then convert. 1 mT is 0.001 T. 1 µWb is 0.000 001 Wb.

Every contactor, relay and solenoid coil makes this field while current flows. The current round its turns gives the coil a north end and a south end. The grip tells you which is which. On AC they swap every half-cycle.

**Rules of thumb:** Reverse the current, and the field turns round. In air, double the current and the field doubles. Round a long straight wire in air, double the distance and the density halves. Two cores carrying the same current out and back make rings that run opposite ways. A little way off, their fields largely cancel.

**Worked example:** The flux density inside a coil is 5 mT. A 0.002 m² hoop held square-on catches 0.005 × 0.002 = 0.000 01 Wb, which is 10 µWb. Tilted 60°, it catches 10 × 0.5 = 5 µWb. The density is still 5 mT, because the coil has not changed.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating flux as the field. Flux is what one loop catches. It changes with the loop's size and tilt, even when the field does not.
- Drawing a wire's field as spokes. It runs round the wire in rings. So a needle lies across the line to the wire.
- Using sin for the tilt. Square-on is 0°. There cos is 1, and the hoop catches the most.
- Thinking a wire's field falls with the square of the distance. It falls in step with the distance: twice as far, half as strong.

interactive.html:
A wire carrying a current, seen end-on, then bent into a loop and a coil, with a hoop to hold in the coil's field. Every value is an example. Inside the coil the density is 5 mT, and each line the hoop catches is 1 µWb.

Each line drawn is 1 µWb. Near a long straight wire, the density in mT is 0.2 × amps ÷ mm.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the hoop's flux halve, with the coil's field still at 5 mT, when you tilt the hoop 60° from square-on.

checks.label: Compasses placed near a long straight current-carrying wire show field lines forming circular loops centred on the wire: every ring is drawn round the wire, and every needle lies along its ring
The right-hand grip: a current into the page makes clockwise rings, so the needle just above the wire points right; reversed it points left; with no current there are no rings
B = μ₀ I ÷ 2πr with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A, which in mT and mm is 0.2 × A ÷ mm: 20 A gives 0.4 mT at 10 mm, 0.2 mT at 20 mm and 0.1 mT at 40 mm, as the needle's readout shows
The magnetic field produced by the coil resembles that of a bar magnet: its lines run one way through the middle and back the other way round the outside, leaving from the end marked N

More turns or more current crowd the lines: 10 turns draw more lines than 6, 20 A more than 10 A, and 2 turns fewer; reversing the current keeps their number; inside a loop the rings from both sides point the same way
Magnetic flux counts the part of the field perpendicular to the hoop's area: square-on the hoop catches the most, tilted less, edge-on none, while the field it sits in stays the same
The hoop lights as many lines as its flux in µWb, to the nearest line, for both hoops at every tilt (10 → 5 at 60°, 20 → 10); past the coil's end the density and the flux fall
Each typed answer and slip is worked from its rule: 20 µWb (slips 10, 20 000 and 0.02), 0.1 mT (slips 0.025, 0.4 and 1.6) and 12 µWb (slips 24, 20.8 and 12 000)

Before a Check no puzzle shows its answer, and a right Check shows it: the needle above the wire points right, the coil's end turns to show N, the wider hoop lights 20 lines, the density shows 5 mT, the needle moves to 40 mm, the tilted hoop lights 12 lines, and the reversed coil swaps N and S
Every demonstration ends 3 to 4.5 s after its screen opens, and every answer's motion within 2.5 s
